title: Rohatsu again
hook: the week of sitting for the awakening

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lhabab Duchen: a debt to a mother, repaid with the teaching. Your line: he came down.

The last night of the week. In a cold Zen hall, nobody has lain down. The candles are low. Legs ache. Someone's stomach growls, loud, and nobody laughs. Then the windows begin to gray, and low in the east, before the sun, one bright point of light hangs over the trees. In Zen tellings, that's the moment: the seeker under the tree looks up at the morning star and wakes. Rohatsu is the week of sitting that ends there. You've stayed through the last night before, and the middle of the week with Mara's army. This year, listen for what tradition says came out of his mouth when it was over.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT OF THE WEEK.` → `ONE BRIGHT POINT IN THE EAST.` → `WHAT DID HE SAY?`

segments.voice: First, the verses. The Dhammapada holds two short verses that the commentary tradition places on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening. He speaks to a builder: the one who keeps putting up the house of a self, life after life. He says he went looking for that builder through many births, and birth again and again was painful. Then the turn, in Max Müller's words: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent or a house. The verse goes on to say the rafters are broken and the ridge-pole shattered. Who is the builder? The commentary reads it as the mind's own craving, the thirst that keeps reaching and keeps making a shelter out of me and mine. It was never an enemy outside. It was a habit, and once it was seen clearly, it couldn't keep building. So why a week of sitting? The house isn't taken down by force. It's seen. And seeing needs stillness, so for a week, from before dawn into the night, people in Zen halls sit and watch the builder at work: the plans, the worries, the little stories of who they are. This week on the path walked the festival year: the wheel set rolling, the rains, the ancestors, the invitation, the gifts, the descent. It ends where the teaching began: one person, sitting still until the morning star.
screen: `TWO VERSES AT THE AWAKENING.` · `THE BUILDER HAS BEEN SEEN.` · `CRAVING BUILDS THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Sit as still as is comfortable and watch for the builder: a plan for later, a worry about someone, a story about yourself. Don't fight it; just notice, there's the builder picking up a plank, and come back to the breath, again and again. When the bell rings, stay a little longer if you can, the way the Zen halls sit through the night; even one more breath counts.
Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the awakening, when tradition says the Buddha saw the morning star. Today's word.
Your line: the morning star. One bright point before sunrise, and a builder seen. A week of festivals, done.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries in Japan and elsewhere, monks and lay practitioners sit an intensive week-long retreat called Rohatsu sesshin, ending on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, sometimes sitting through the final night.

chat.says: Who is the builder the Buddha talks to when he wakes up?
options: The commentary reads it as craving, the habit that keeps building me and mine.
It's Mara, an enemy outside him who kept building traps to stop his awakening.
It's the body, which he vowed to starve until it stopped asking for anything.
chat.meaning: In the Dhammapada verses tradition places at the awakening, the builder of the house is seen; the commentary reads it as craving, not an outside enemy.

notes: Dhammapada 154 opening quoted from Müller (1881); confirm wording exactly ('But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again.').
Dh 153–154 paraphrased: seeking the house-builder through many births; rafters broken, ridge-pole shattered. Identifying the builder as craving (tanha) follows the commentarial reading; confirm.
'The commentary tradition places [these verses] on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening': confirm phrasing; some traditions place a different utterance first.
Morning star at the awakening attributed to Zen / East Asian tellings.
Original: Devanagari for Pali gahakaraka (गहकारक); confirm spelling.
'Ten more minutes' comes from the outline's practice ('sit an extra ten minutes'); it is an invitation, not a claim.
Week end (days 1415–1421): the teach's close looks back over the week. Earlier Rohatsu days (y2 691, y3 1058) used the last night and the Padhana Sutta; this day uses the house-builder verses.

Editor: the verse itself does not name craving as the builder; attributed that reading to the commentary (teach and myth reveal). Replaced "the awakening they all point back to" (overclaims Ullambana and the descent) with a plain close.
